_meta.purpose: Every number the product puts on screen lives here with a source. Plan rule 2: never invent a number.
_meta.how_to_use: Replace each entry where verified=false with a real cited figure, fill source and date, then set verified=true. The UI shows an amber 'unsourced' badge for any figure derived from an unverified entry, and a banner while any remain.
_meta.warning_to_the_team: Entries verified on 2026-10-18 carry a real citation in their `source` field and the assumptions behind them in `note`. Read the note before quoting a figure to a judge: several entries are published METHODS applied to our own stated assumptions, not published end numbers, and the note says which is which.

e_out_small.source: Derived from the EcoLogits methodology (GenAI Impact, 'LLM Inference' methodology page, https://ecologits.ai/latest/methodology/llm_inference/, and the constants in ecologits/impacts/llm.py, https://github.com/genai-impact/ecologits). Published constants used: GPU energy per output token = alpha*exp(beta*B)*P_active + gamma with alpha=1.1665e-06, beta=-1.1206e-02, gamma=4.0529e-05, batch B=64; non-GPU server power 1.2 kW over 8 installed GPUs; GPU memory 80 GB; 16-bit weights; latency per token = 6.785e-04*P_active + 3.119e-04*B + 1.9474e-02 s; PUE 1.09-1.20 (EcoLogits provider table).
e_out_small.note: OUR ASSUMPTION, not the source's: the small class spans 3-20 billion ACTIVE parameters. Low bound = 3B active, dense (total = active), PUE 1.09. High bound = 20B active in a sparse model whose TOTAL parameters are 4x active (more GPUs must hold the weights), PUE 1.20. The formulas, constants and PUE range are published; the parameter band and the 4x active-to-total ratio are ours and are why this stays wide. Closed-model parameter counts are estimates, so treat this as an order-of-magnitude band, not a measurement. EcoLogits assumes A100/H100-class hardware and excludes embodied impact from this figure.

e_out_medium.source: Derived from the EcoLogits methodology, same published constants and PUE range as e_out_small (https://ecologits.ai/latest/methodology/llm_inference/).
e_out_medium.note: OUR ASSUMPTION: the medium class spans 20-100 billion active parameters. Low = 20B active dense at PUE 1.09; high = 100B active with total = 4x active at PUE 1.20. See e_out_small for what is published and what is ours. Ranges for adjacent classes overlap on purpose: the classes are not cleanly separable when parameter counts are estimates.

e_out_large.source: Derived from the EcoLogits methodology, same published constants and PUE range as e_out_small (https://ecologits.ai/latest/methodology/llm_inference/).
e_out_large.note: OUR ASSUMPTION: the large class spans 100-500 billion active parameters. Low = 100B active dense at PUE 1.09; high = 500B active with total = 4x active at PUE 1.20, which needs 64 GPUs under the methodology's memory rule and drives the top of the band. Sanity check against the same formulas: a 405B dense model comes out at about 9 Wh per 1000 output tokens. Frontier model sizes are not published, so this is the widest band in the file and should be presented as such.

e_in.source: Design decision, plan section 6.2: output-centred model, input weight defaults to 0
e_in.note: Deliberately zero. This is a modelling choice, not an empirical claim. Add a labelled sensitivity scenario with a small non-zero weight once a source exists, and say on screen that input energy is excluded.

e_cache_read.source: Design decision, plan section 6.2: cache reads weighted near zero
e_cache_read.note: Cache reads are most of the tokens in coding-agent sessions but use little energy. Modelling choice, not an empirical claim.

e_cache_write.source: Design decision, plan section 6.2: optional small term, default 0
e_cache_write.note: Modelling choice, not an empirical claim.

WI.source: Siddik, M.A.B., Shehabi, A. and Marston, L. (2021), 'The environmental footprint of data centers in the United States', Environmental Research Letters 16(6) 064017, https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/abfba1
WI.note: SCOPE, and this is the figure most easily overclaimed: the LOW bound (1800 mL/kWh = 1.8 L/kWh) is ON-SITE COOLING ONLY, the paper's typical data-centre cooling requirement of 1.8 m3/MWh. The HIGH bound (7100 mL/kWh = 7.1 L/kWh) is the paper's US national average for ON-SITE PLUS OFF-SITE, i.e. including the water consumed generating the electricity: the paper reports that 1 MWh of data-centre electricity consumption requires about 7.1 m3 of water in total (of which about 5.3 m3/MWh is off-site, from electricity generation). They differ by about 4x, so never present the high bound as cooling water. Both are 2018 US averages; water intensity is highly regional and the paper says so.

grid_fallback.source: US EPA, eGRID2023 (data year 2023, Revision 2, released 12 June 2025), https://www.epa.gov/egrid/download-data - subregion sheet SRL23, annual CO2-equivalent total output emission rates for the three eGRID subregions that cover the PJM footprint: SRVC 596.326 lb/MWh, RFCE 599.170 lb/MWh, RFCW 916.054 lb/MWh.
grid_fallback.note: Range is the min and max of those three subregions converted at 0.45359237 g per lb (270.5 and 415.5 gCO2e/kWh). eGRID's own PJM balancing-authority value, 719.405 lb/MWh = 326.3 gCO2e/kWh, sits inside the range, which is the point of the range. Same basis as the EF entries below (direct combustion), so the fallback and the live calculation are comparable. Annual average, not hourly and not marginal. Always labelled 'fallback value, not live' on screen.

EF._note: Emissions factor per fuel, used to turn the PJM fuel mix into a carbon intensity (plan section 9.2). ONE source for every fuel: US EPA eGRID2023 (data year 2023, Revision 2, released 12 June 2025), https://www.epa.gov/egrid/download-data. Each range is the min and max of the annual CO2-equivalent fuel-specific output emission rate across the three eGRID subregions covering PJM (RFCE, RFCW, SRVC), converted at 0.45359237 g per lb. eGRID's PJM balancing-authority values fall inside each range.

COL.source: EPA eGRID2023 rev2, SRL23 annual CO2e coal output emission rate: SRVC 2122.213, RFCW 2228.280, RFCE 2408.594 lb/MWh
COL.note: Coal. PJM balancing-authority value 2232.587 lb/MWh = 1012.7 gCO2e/kWh.

NG.source: EPA eGRID2023 rev2, SRL23 annual CO2e gas output emission rate: RFCE 855.982, RFCW 882.155, SRVC 955.244 lb/MWh
NG.note: Natural gas. PJM balancing-authority value 867.973 lb/MWh = 393.7 gCO2e/kWh.

OIL.source: EPA eGRID2023 rev2, SRL23 annual CO2e oil output emission rate: SRVC 1442.956, RFCE 1795.787, RFCW 1997.323 lb/MWh
OIL.note: Petroleum. PJM balancing-authority value 1922.897 lb/MWh = 872.2 gCO2e/kWh. EPA notes oil-fired output rates can be distorted where a plant runs little but emits a lot, which is part of why this band is wide.

NUC.source: EPA eGRID2023 rev2: eGRID reports combustion emissions only, so non-combustion generation has a zero output emission rate
NUC.note: Nuclear. Zero on a DIRECT COMBUSTION basis by construction, not a claim that nuclear is lifecycle-zero. On a lifecycle basis (e.g. IPCC AR5 Annex III) it is roughly 12 gCO2eq/kWh. Switching this file to a lifecycle basis means replacing EVERY fuel here from one lifecycle source and changing _basis.

WND.source: EPA eGRID2023 rev2: combustion emissions only, so non-combustion generation has a zero output emission rate
WND.note: Wind. Zero on a direct combustion basis by construction; roughly 11 gCO2eq/kWh on a lifecycle basis. See NUC.

SUN.source: EPA eGRID2023 rev2: combustion emissions only, so non-combustion generation has a zero output emission rate
SUN.note: Solar. Zero on a direct combustion basis by construction; roughly 41-48 gCO2eq/kWh on a lifecycle basis. See NUC.

WAT.source: EPA eGRID2023 rev2: combustion emissions only, so non-combustion generation has a zero output emission rate
WAT.note: Hydro. Zero on a direct combustion basis by construction; roughly 24 gCO2eq/kWh on a lifecycle basis and highly site-specific. See NUC.

OTH.source: EPA eGRID2023 rev2: bounded by the gas low and coal high of the same subregion set (388.3 and 1092.5 gCO2e/kWh)
OTH.note: Other / unknown, and pumped storage, which the feed does not break out. eGRID publishes no fuel-specific rate for 'other fossil', so this band deliberately spans from the cleanest gas rate to the dirtiest coal rate in the same source. Wide on purpose: if much generation lands here, say so rather than reporting a tight number.

va_dc.unit: billion gallons of water per year (2023, Virginia data centre industry)
va_dc.source: Virginia Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission (JLARC), 'Data Centers in Virginia', Report 598, December 2024, chapter 5, https://jlarc.virginia.gov/pdfs/reports/Rpt598.pdf
va_dc.note: JLARC's own words: 'In 2023, the data center industry used an estimated 2.1 billion gallons of water, with just over a third coming from reclaimed water instead of new withdrawals', and that this was 'less than 0.5 percent of total state withdrawals'. Quote BOTH halves: the reclaimed-water share and the 0.5 percent, or the figure overstates the pressure on Virginia's water. A point estimate, not a range, so no spread is implied. For the energy side of the same report: JLARC's independent forecast has unconstrained Virginia power demand doubling within ten years, driven primarily by data centre growth (chapter 3).

ACL2025.unit: % reduction in measured inference energy per sample
ACL2025.source: Poddar, S., Koley, P., Misra, J., Podder, S., Balani, N., Ganguly, N. and Ghosh, S. (2025), 'Brevity is the soul of sustainability: Characterizing LLM response lengths', Findings of ACL 2025, arXiv:2506.08686, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08686 - section 5.2, 'Effects on Energy Consumption'
ACL2025.note: These are the figures the paper MEASURES (CodeCarbon, mWh per sample, averaged over its datasets): about 28% energy reduction for its MinAns prompt strategy and about 26% for PredResLen, with BM25-InContext reducing energy for no model. Quote 26-28%, not the paper's own wider claims: the abstract says 'energy optimization between 25-60%' and the introduction says 'up to 58% reduction in energy consumption', and the body does not derive either. The paper's 60%-ish figure is a RESPONSE LENGTH reduction (MinAns, about 60% shorter; PredResLen 53% on average), not energy. 12 decoder-only LLMs across 5 datasets. If a judge checks the paper, section 5.2 is the line that supports what we say.
